meta.title: TORFL A2 Basic — Russian
meta.subtitle: 750 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Russian → English (see the Russian, recall the meaning) and English → Russian (see an English meaning, recall the Russian). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 750 words for the Basic level (Базовый уровень, ТБУ) of TORFL, the Test of Russian as a Foreign Language (ТРКИ), the Russian state examination, which corresponds to CEFR A2. TORFL's Basic level is aligned to A1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand sentences and frequently used expressions related to areas of most immediate relevance' — a learner here is able to manage simple, routine exchanges of information on familiar matters — personal and family information, shopping, the local area, work — and to describe in simple terms their background, their surroundings and what they immediately need. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: TORFL's lexical minimum for each level is published as a book under copyright rather than as an open list, so this deck is not the exam board's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 295 of the 750 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — relatives and the people around you, work and study, clothes and shopping, more food and cooking, the furniture of a home, the town, the countryside and the four points of the compass, travel, health and the body, feelings and character, free time, telling what happened and when, giving an opinion, the numbers to a million, and the everyday verbs of moving, dressing and doing — and the other 455 are the commonest remaining words of everyday Russian, taken from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles and counted by the WHOLE word, every case and every tense added together, since a list of word forms ranks книгу above книга. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. Every headword and every form is printed with its stress mark, as Russian dictionaries for learners print them, because Russian stress is free and moves (рука́, ру́ку) and nothing in the spelling shows it; the example sentences are printed as they were written, without stress. 170 of the verbs are taught as aspect pairs on one card, imperfective first (де́лать / сде́лать), each with its own conjugation, since a Russian verb is learnt as a pair; the verbs of motion that make round trips (ходи́ть, е́здить) are cards of their own beside идти́ and е́хать, because the difference is the lesson. The 325 nouns show their gender, their genitive singular and their nominative plural, from which the rest of the declension follows, and every word that inflects has its whole table behind the All forms fold. 1 of the entries are set phrases rather than single words — день рождения. Every word carries three real example sentences, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. There is no transliteration: learn the alphabet first with the Russian alphabet deck, which is the first deck in this collection. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, forms, stress and aspect: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
